definition: In machine learning, a neural network (NN) or artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the structure and functions of biological neural networks.
details: A neural network consists of connected units or nodes called artificial neurons, which loosely model the neurons in the brain. These are connected by edges, which model the synapses in the brain. Each artificial neuron receives signals from connected neurons, then processes them and sends a signal to other connected neurons. The "signal" is a real number, and the output of each neuron is computed by some non-linear function of the totality of its inputs, called the activation function. The strength of the signal at each connection is determined by a weight, which adjusts as part of the training process. Groups of neurons are aggregated into layers. Each layer performs a transformation on its inputs. Signals travel from the first layer (the input layer) to the last layer (the output layer), typically passing through multiple intermediate layers (hidden layers). A network is typically called a deep neural network if it has at least two hidden layers. Deep neural networks are capable of learning sophisticated hierarchical representations. explainer.lead: A neural network is the core computational model behind most modern machine learning, built from connected artificial neurons. It matters because stacking these units with nonlinear activations lets models learn complex patterns directly from data.

tiers.eli5: It's a web of tiny decision-makers passing numbers to each other, and by adjusting how strongly they listen to each other, the whole web gets better at a task.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers build networks from layers of units joined by weighted edges and train the weights so outputs match targets. A common pitfall is underestimating how much the activation function and weight initialisation affect whether training converges.
tiers.paperLevel: A network consists of connected units (artificial neurons) joined by edges; each neuron receives signals (real numbers), processes them, and sends an output computed by a nonlinear activation function of the totality of its inputs, with connection strengths given by weights. Single-unit learning was shown by the perceptron on simple classifications.

explainer.example: A network takes pixel values as input signals, each neuron sums its weighted inputs and applies a nonlinear activation, and the weights are adjusted so the output matches the label.
